For example, it may be stressful for families to spend the focus of meals on the child’s eating behaviors. These strategies tend to give children little control and may create power dynamics at the table. Escape extinction such as nonremoval of the spoon can be aversive for the parent to implement, child to experience, and negatively impact caregiver-child interactions. Promising cognitive behavioral approaches that deviate from traditional operant conditioning behavioral approaches are emerging. A pilot study by using a multifamily group cognitive behavioral approach with 11 participants ages 8–12 with ASD with IQ at or higher than 80 showed high participant satisfaction. completed a feasibility study on a cognitive behavioral therapy approach to target avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, with clinicians rating 85% of the 17 participants who completed the study as much or very much improved. However, both of these approaches focused on older children with a cognitive level capable of engaging in more complex tasks such as monitoring their thoughts, feelings, and /or sensations and engaging in aspects of cognitive restructuring. Alternative approaches are still needed for younger children or individuals with lower developmental levels. A second gap is the relative lack of studies focused on outpatient treatments for feeding; those that exist have small sample sizes. The majority of published studies have focused on day treatment and inpatient treatments ranging from 11 to 46 intervention days (see ). While they are associated with positive outcomes, there are challenges. Day treatment program and inpatient hospitalizations are expensive, disrupt family life ( ), and may present challenges when trying to generalize behavioral techniques to the home setting. Given the intensive nature of inpatient and day treatment programs, there may be longer waitlists since only a few patients can be treated at one time. It is also unclear whether these programs can reduce the stress families feel around feeding, especially once they return to home settings. With behavioral approaches, strategies used may be specific for the client and difficult to take a universal approach with all children in the family. Among studies focused on outpatient feeding treatment, study sizes are small. For example, used an escape extinction technique by continuously placing a small amount of food on a child’s lips or inside of his mouth every 5–10 seconds. A second randomized controlled study of 21 patients found that the 73% of patients who completed the study were all able to transition from tube to oral feeding after undergoing a 6-month interdisciplinary outpatient feeding program ( ). A third study that specifically focused on children with ASD found decreased parental stress but no changes to mealtime behavior during the 8-week intervention ( ). showed decreased parental concern and increased enjoyment of food by participants in a group treatment but the study size was small ( n = 20). Further studies that incorporate parental experiences with larger sample sizes are needed. A third gap in the literature is the lack of research on the outcomes of clinical treatment approaches that are commonly used in clinical practice and offer an alternative to escape extinction and operant conditioning compliance approaches. For example, the Sensory Oral Motor Sequences (SOS) Approach ( ) to feeding is grounded in the use of systematic desensitization and learning and has been used in multiple clinical settings. This latter presentation presented some preliminary feasibility data including cost of treatment and outcomes. These pilot studies are promising, although two of them are unpublished. Of note, a significant difference between the SOS Approach and traditional behavioral approaches is that in the SOS Approach, children are in charge of how much they engage in the systematic desensitization whereas in traditional behavioral approaches, children typically obey and follow commands. Thus, the SOS Approach was chosen as the basis of the Picnic Group intervention as it offers a classical conditioning strategy for addressing feeding. Further, its focus on using playful interactions as tools for learning are in line with child development. This approach allows for intrinsic motivation around learning. The approach also allows for positive child-caregiver interactions and a return to a trajectory where children learn that mealtimes are a positive shared social experience. Another frequently used and understudied approach is the Get Permission Approach (Klein; www.getpermissionapproach.com ). This approach helps guide caregivers to read children’s cues and support them while helping their children learn to become “happy, self-directed eaters who enjoy eating, are confident in their eating skills and are internally motivated to eat enough” (Klein). Aspects of this approach were also chosen to be used in the Picnic Group as it helps caregivers feel successful. The approach changes the dynamics of the parent-child relationship in feeding such that both parties may change their thoughts, feelings, and behaviors around mealtime. In the , exposure as a form of learning is also used to help children learn to experience joy and confidence in eating. In Satter’s model, meals are considered the repeated neutral exposure to learn to enjoy foods, provide emotional and social reassurance, and social experience ( ). In brief, in the Division of Responsibility, Satter posits it is the adult’s responsibility to choose what is served, where it is served, and when it is served while it is the child’s responsibility to choose whether and how much food is eaten. This level of control that children have is similar to that of the SOS Approach. This approach signifies a significant deviation from behavioral approaches that focus on compliance based on number of bites eaten and focuses instead on children learning how to have positive relationships with feeding. However, the other components of the SOS Approach and Get Permission Approach were felt to be necessary to include in treatment with children with PFD so that children and their caregivers had systematic approaches to exploring novel or not-yet-preferred foods that could be causing them anxiety or other negative feelings. Food chaining ( ) is another strategy that is commonly used but understudied. There is one retrospective study available with 10 participants ( ), and more are needed. Food chaining links a preferred food to a new or nonpreferred food by changing one sensory property of the food at a time. For example, food chaining can be used to progress a child who only eats applesauce to raw apple slices, by modifying one aspect of the food at a time, waiting for habituation or pleasurable associations to the new variation, and then changing another aspect of the food the next time the child is working on exposures (see for sample). More research is needed on feeding protocols that may address the multiple factors that impact eating (e.g., anxiety, mechanics, sensory aversions, skill deficits), as well as the broader areas of a child’s life that are impacted by feeding problems (e.g., caregiver-child interactions during mealtime, negative associations with mealtime). These components were chosen as they help children learn how to enjoy food through a habituation and systematic desensitization model, reframe mealtimes, and foster more natural child-caregiver interactions around feeding. The current study focuses on a retrospective review of outcomes of the children who were treated by an interdisciplinary outpatient group program that uses alternative techniques to more limited escape extinction models. The Picnic Group draws from cognitive behavioral principles, the SOS Approach to Feeding ( ), the Get Permission Approach (Klein, www.getpermissionapproach.com ), , , 2023), Food Chaining ( ), and traditional oral sensory techniques. The Picnic Group used in this study has been used in our clinical setting for 15 years with children with a variety of medical and developmental disorders who have commercial and public insurance, which suggests the program is feasible to implement in a pediatric hospital outpatient setting. Our clinical impression is that this integrative method is useful for decreasing parental stress and improving children’s abilities to tolerate and enjoy a wider range of foods, but this has not been examined quantitatively. Our patients consist of a diverse group of children with isolated feeding problems as well as children with comorbid medical or developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorders. Advantages of our program include that it is easier for caregivers to implement, it has a broader focus, addresses parental stress and parent-child relationships, and taps into the children’s intrinsic motivation to interact with food. This has improved generalizability and sustainability of treatment benefits. Picnic Group Intervention Program At our large regional pediatric hospital, our 12-week Picnic Group uses an interdisciplinary treatment approach that draws from cognitive behavioral principles and sensory integration principles. A theoretical model of the approach has been illustrated in . Techniques focus on changing the negative associations children and caregivers have built around mealtime through: classical conditioning (e.g., by increasing pleasurable interactions with each other, using playful systematic desensitization approaches to decrease anxiety and aversion to the food); addressing the impact of sensory needs on feeding; addressing caregivers’ automatic thoughts, behaviors, and feelings around their children’s feeding; addressing the impact of feeding on the family system; and using peer modeling for social learning and support for both the children and parents/caregivers. Medical providers, dietitians, speech-language pathologists, and psychologists diagnose and treat the medical, nutritional, motor, sensory, and behavioral components of feeding problems seen in our population. Participants attend the hour-long group sessions once weekly for a total of 12 weeks. Children participate in a child’s group while caregivers participate in a caregiver group that is held simultaneously in a room with a one-way mirror. Child Approach Theoretically, in our view children’s nondesired behaviors occur in part because they have negative automatic thoughts and feelings about food or feeding, rather than misbehavior (see ). For example, when they see a nonpreferred food, they may have thoughts like “I hate dinner” or “This is going to be horrible” or “I can’t do it.” They may have feelings such as “This is scary.” Their behaviors may look like hiding, tantrumming, crying, or saying things like “I won’t eat it” or “This is yucky.” To target children’s negative automatic thoughts and feelings, children’s food selectivity is addressed through a cognitive behavioral lens, which includes aspects of the SOS Approach to Feeding ( ), the Get Permission Approach (Klein, www.getpermissionapproach.com ), , , 2023), and Food Chaining ( ). The cognitive behavioral strategies are based on classical conditioning, systematic desensitization, and habituation. The group modeling is based on social learning theory. Caregiver Approach Caregivers receive psychoeducation, cognitive behavioral therapy, family systems interventions, and parent-to-parent support to help facilitate generalization of feeding progress to the home environment, increase predictability of mealtimes, increase child-caregiver interactions during mealtime, and increase the enjoyment of family mealtime. Our approach differs from traditional operant conditioning models in most feeding treatment research that tend to rely more exclusively on operant conditioning strategies that emphasize aversive escape extinction and consistent rewarding of each bite. It also reduces the need for the caregiver to act as an authoritative disciplinarian during the meal. Instead, the caregiver can focus instead on enjoying the food and mealtime with their child rather than count how many bites the child takes. In addition, our services are provided in a group format to capitalize on peer modeling, which is also different from most published studies on feeding treatment. Hypotheses In this paper, we compare ratings between Week 12 of intervention and baseline. This study examined three primary hypotheses: Hypothesis 1: Our hypothesis is that there were fewer feeding problems and negative feeding behaviors posttreatment than at baseline. Rationale: We think children were displaying problematic feeding behaviors due to their thoughts and feelings related to feeding stimuli, rather than noncompliance or misbehavior. This hypothesis is based on research on factors that impact anxiety, development, learning, and preliminary data that make up components of the Picnic Group. By focusing on the feelings, habituation, reframing, and strategies to pair positive interactions with foods, children will have decreased anxiety about the food and therefore show fewer problematic behaviors. Hypothesis 2: Our hypothesis is that the number of foods children are willing to engage with at Week 12 is higher than the number of foods at Week 1. Rationale: We think that children are more likely to engage with food when they learn strategies to approach new or not-yet-preferred foods and practice habituating to each step while interacting with the food in a pleasurable way. This hypothesis is based on research on learning, intrinsic motivation, and the role of habituation in anxiety treatment. Hypothesis 3: Our hypothesis is that caregivers’ own strain related to oral feeding concerns will be lower at Week 12 than at Week 1. Rationale: Our program addresses caregiver feelings and provides caregivers with tools to address their own automatic thoughts, perspectives, and feelings. Based on cognitive behavioral therapy, when changing someone’s behaviors and automatic thoughts, we expect to see a change in their feelings which, in this situation, we are examining as caregiver strain. Methods Participants Between January 1, 2004 and August 31, 2014, 93 children ages 30 months to 11 years ( ) were seen by the Feeding Team for group treatment. We received approval from the hospital Institutional Review Board for conducting a retrospective analysis on these patients’ measures. Patients all exhibited feeding problems. Some children had isolated feeding problems. Other children also had comorbid medical or developmental disorders. These diagnoses include developmental delay, cystic fibrosis, ASD, craniofacial abnormalities, gastro esophageal reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, food allergies, anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder inattentive subtype, hyperactivity/impulsivity subtype and combined subtypes, genetic syndromes such as Down Syndrome and DiGeorge syndrome, cardiac defects, history of prematurity, sensory integration disorder, and short gut syndrome. Approximately 45% of the sample had an ASD. Although there is considerable heterogeneity of underlying diagnoses as well as overall severity of feeding problems, the children were similar in the phase of intervention required and were included because they were representative of the clinic population that consists of varying diagnoses. Some children were utilizing nasogastric or gastric tubes for nutritional and/or hydration needs at the time they attended group. All children could separate from their caregivers, attend to motivating, tabletop activities for 30–40 minutes without one-to-one support from an adult, and were judged clinically to have potential benefit from peer modeling, based on caregiver or therapist reports. Patients were not selected randomly. All patients received the same topics in treatment with some variability in order of topics. All patients who received treatment and completed pre- and post-intervention assessments are included in the review. Groups consisted of children with Latinx/Hispanic, Asian, Black/African-American and White backgrounds ( ). Non-English-speaking children and/or families participated in our groups through interpretation. Most participants were boys (73/93 or 78%). Patient characteristics are presented in . Patients all had feeding problems, although some children with swallowing problems or predominantly oral motor problems were typically referred to individual treatment to better address those difficulties. Some participants had previously participated in individual or group feeding therapy with an occupational therapist or speech-language pathologist or had had consultations with a gastroenterologist, registered dietitian or behavior therapist. Feeding History Survey This questionnaire was created to gather information from families about the child’s feeding problems and experiences starting at birth. The data collected from this survey yields the number of feeding problems indicated by the caregiver from a checklist of possibilities. The feeding problems on this measure are specific to the child and are considered negative behaviors. The caregiver indicates whether the behavior is present. Children’s Eating Behavior Inventory This measure asks caregivers to record the frequency of different eating and mealtime behaviors. Caregivers also indicated whether the behavior was problematic to them. Although normative data is reported in the article accompanying the inventory, for our purposes, we recorded the number of behaviors reported as a problem by the caregivers ( ). The types of behaviors on this measure range from positive to negative and include other family members in addition to the child. The caregiver completing this measure is asked to report the frequency of all behaviors and whether the behavior constitutes a problem from their perspective. Feeding Caregiver Strain Questionnaire This measure was adapted from the Caregiver Strain Questionnaire ( ) that was originally intended to measure the impact that living with a child with emotional and behavioral problems had on the family and caregiver. For most items, “emotional or behavioral problem” was replaced with “feeding difficulties.” For our purposes, caregivers were asked to focus on the past 6 weeks instead of past 6 months. We reported the total score for this instrument, reversing the value of one item. Bites Swallowed A trained assistant tracked and documented the level of interaction with food items as they were presented at each treatment session, and whether each food item reached the swallowing stage at that session. These results were reviewed and confirmed by one of two clinicians who were present throughout the treatment sessions. A standard test menu with foods from different food groups and with different textures is offered at both Week 1 and Week 12 to facilitate comparison. Statistical Methodology We reported the median and range for both baseline and 12-week measurements ( ). To compare outcomes between baseline and the 12-week follow-up, we used the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test. Each p -value was adjusted for multiple comparisons via the Bonferroni method. Hedges’s g is reported as a general effect size measure for differences in measurements, with rough interpretation of Hedges’s g as small (0.2), moderate (~0.5), and large (~0.8) ( ). Spearman correlations were calculated to assess the association between demographic and diagnoses with treatment outcomes. A linear regression was also conducted to examine whether demographics or diagnoses were associated with differences in outcomes. Procedures On average, each family in the group brings in two foods per week for all children in the group to share, with one food that is already familiar or preferred, and another food that is new, in progress, or not yet preferred. To start changing the children’s automatic thoughts on food with ones they like versus dislike, each week revolves around a particular theme based on shape (e.g., foods that can be cut into triangles), color (e.g., foods that are green), or taste (e.g., citrus or sour foods). This allows both children and caregivers to start discussing foods with other characteristics other than like or dislike and allows for nonjudgmental descriptive words for various foods. During these sessions, children typically engage in exposures with 8 to 10 foods per week in session, depending on group size or attendance. Caregivers are also instructed to expose their children to new, in progress, and not-yet-preferred foods at mealtime at home. New foods are ones that children have not been exposed to before. In-progress foods are those that children have started engaging in exposures with. Not-yet-preferred foods are foods that children have tried but may not like yet. Families are generally guided to have 75% of the meal consist of familiar or preferred foods, and 25% of the meal consisting of a new, in progress, or not-yet-preferred food. Families are generally guided to have 75% of the meal consist of familiar or preferred foods, and 25% of the meal consisting of a new, in progress, or not-yet-preferred food. During the classical conditioning approach exposure technique, instead of having an immediate expectation to consume a new food, children are presented with multiple intermediate steps in a fear hierarchy, such as smelling the food, touching the unfamiliar food, or kissing the food. Children have control over the pace of moving through the hierarchy using play and exploration until children are habituated and not as fearful of eating the new food, based on their affect or behaviors. The process lets them build positive associations with the food. While the majority of interactions are based on classical conditioning principles, the approach also incorporates aspects of operant conditioning at times, such as intermittent use of social rewards such as verbal encouragement to reinforce approximations to the goal. For example, a child may hear “Great job touching the carrot” or receive a “High Five.” At times, children may receive other rewards for their efforts. For example, if a family is having challenges with motivation in the home setting, they may track the number of times a child engages with a step on a fear hierarchy such as smelling a food or making teeth marks in the food. A predetermined reward may have been discussed with the family, such as reading an extra book at bedtime. Broadly, however, the goal is for children and families to be trained to enjoy exploring food such that the positive experience (e.g., play) is presented simultaneously with the food in a classical conditioning presentation, rather than to eat for the purposes of receiving rewards. Thus, in our program, the food is considered the stimulus and presented simultaneously with pleasurable experiences. Most sessions are facilitated by an occupational therapist and a speech-language pathologist, with occasional psychologist participation. From the moment children arrive, the emphasis is on creating the positive association between mealtime routine and pleasure. When transitioning from the waiting room to the clinic room, clinicians already engage in pleasurable activities such as blowing bubbles or singing songs to decrease stress and increase regulation. The session begins with a 10-minute sensory warm-up activity such as smelling various food odors and guessing the item or using hands to paint with shaving cream. We often read a story related to food or eating and the children are encouraged to participate by filling in words or turning pages. This activity is followed by hand-washing and oral warm-ups utilizing an oral motor tool. Children then go to the mealtime table. At the table, children engage in a routine that is also intended to keep children feeling regulated before engaging more in exposures. Children follow a routine of examining and passing each food item around. Each child takes some of the food item onto his, her, or their plate, typically with their hands or utensil. Children, the speech-language, and occupational therapists then playfully interact with the food using a systematic desensitization and hierarchical approach. In keeping with the tenets of the SOS Approach ( ), children are encouraged to slowly increase level of interaction with the foods, such as touching the food with their fingers, smelling the food, bringing food close to mouth, blowing food near mouth into an “all done” or “bye-bye” bowl, touching the food to lips or “kissing” the food, licking the food, making teeth marks into the food, taking a bite of food and spitting it into the “all-done” bowl, taking a bite of food and chewing it before spitting it into the “all-done” bowl, or chewing and then swallowing the food. Children and adults at the table are encouraged to be as creative and silly as they would like as they engage in their food exploration, emphasizing the pleasurable quality of the food interaction. For example, if the step they are working on is bringing the food closer to their mouth, they might place the food on the back of their hand and blow it off. If they are working on bite pressure, they might hold the food between their teeth like a puppy holds a bone and make barking noises. Therapists encourage increased interaction with the food based on the child’s responses, peer modeling, and giving some autonomy. For example, a therapist might say, “Should we touch the food to our chin or our lips next?” The children move onto the next step if they have habituated to the step they are on and

For example, a therapist might say, “Should we touch the food to our chin or our lips next?” The children move onto the next step if they have habituated to the step they are on and are enjoying that level of interaction. Children are never forced to progress to a particular step. If they have an aversive reaction to a step, they go back to the previous step until they have fully habituated and ideally, can enjoy that step. The child’s level of interaction with the food item is monitored and tracked. Children’s automatic thoughts are addressed by focusing on reframing comments like “I don’t like it” to “I’m not used to it yet” and “I’m learning about this food.” Similarly, instead of viewing food dichotomously as like/dislike, children are taught to think about foods on multiple dimensions (e.g., crunchy versus soft), and what they can do with the food instead of just “I can’t eat it.” At the end of the therapeutic meal, children are expected to engage in an end routine. They kiss or blow their remaining food into the “all done” or “bye-bye” bowl. They then clear their plates, wash their hands, and receive the “report card,” which details their achievements during the session. Parents are encouraged to continue food explorations throughout the intervening week, also engaging in a beginning, middle, and end routine to the mealtime with emphasis on pleasurable interactions with foods that may fall within the theme of the week, or other food the family is eating. They do not need to be the exact same foods as the ones practiced in the clinic session. The focus is on employing food exploration strategies in as many meals as possible so that children learn to generalize the process for engaging in new foods, rather than specific food themselves. On most weeks, while children are in the session with an occupational therapist and speech-language therapist, parents are in their own group in an adjacent room and can watch their children participate in the group. The psychologist provides cognitive behavioral strategies and family systems–based group therapy. The psychologist discusses behavior management, including learning the antecedents and consequences associated with desired and undesired behaviors and links these to potential thoughts and emotions. The group explores changing familial patterns of behaviors at mealtimes, monitoring caregivers’ emotions and feelings that emerge during mealtimes, learning adult coping techniques during mealtime stress, reframing negative cognitions (automatic thoughts) during mealtime, reducing parent-child conflict related to food and improving family systems functioning during mealtime to facilitate carry-over from hospital to home environments. Parents are taught to recognize and understand symptoms of anxiety and sensory aversions, SOS, the Satter Eating Competence Model, and Food Chaining ( ) approaches, and systematic desensitization techniques to address their children’s anxiety and sensory aversions. See for a sample list of topics. The order of topics may shift depending on provider availability. In terms of addressing automatic thoughts, if parents have an automatic thought such as, “She would never eat that” or “He doesn’t eat fish,” they may be guided to formulate an alternate thought, such as, “She is still learning to accept jicama” or “He doesn’t eat fish YET.” If a parent personalizes or overgeneralizes a situation, such as “He won’t eat for me,” parents may be guided to reframe the situation as “He is nervous and is working on eggs” or “He is not eating this yet.” To reframe fear of a food with a child, they might say, “We’re still learning about apples. We’re learning about how it looks, how it smells, etc.” “It’s small and white and hard. For example, a parent may state “I’m a bad parent” as a result of negative messages from others and themselves that their children’s weight and eating issues are their fault. During group sessions, the clinicians and other parents help the parent reframe these thoughts and gain self-compassionate insight. In terms of behavior, parents are guided to offer preferred food along with nonpreferred food to emphasize the idea that both foods are pleasurable, increase likelihood children will eat something at the meal and reduce refusal behaviors, and reduce parental stress about how much the child eats. This study takes a first step at examining the potential impact of a 12-week interdisciplinary treatment program that involves both children and caregivers. Consistent with hypotheses, results of this study suggest children in Picnic Groups showed symptom improvement during the 12-week course and caregivers report less caregiver strain. Caregivers of children with developmental disabilities indicate the greatest decrease in caregiver strain by Week 12. This study has several strengths. The study addresses the gap in literature by examining the use of a treatment program that addresses the potential thoughts, feelings, and learning needed to enjoy food. The program uses classical conditioning strategies such as systematic desensitization and habituation by increasing pleasurable food and mealtime experiences, while still incorporating aspects of operant conditioning to reward efforts, and cognitive behavioral principles to target family functioning and the negative thoughts that are associated with mealtime. In contrast, many other studies to date have focused more exclusively on operant conditioning techniques such as aversive escape extinction approaches and eating to receive rewards (e.g., see review by ). With respect to the reported feeding-related problems, types of problems that were improved upon include tolerance of the sight or smell of non-preferred foods on the table, as well as willingness to touch, smell, or lick novel or non-preferred food items. In this manner, children are progressively desensitized to these foods, allowing them to gradually work towards biting, chewing, and swallowing the food items while maintaining autonomy for what they put inside their mouth. This study found increased ability to work up the food hierarchy. While there is sometimes concern that children may not reach the eventual goal of biting and chewing food if they were not forced to, our participants were able to reach the stage of biting and chewing foods at the 12 th session. A potential benefit of this progressive hierarchical approach is that “trying” new foods can feel more manageable and predictable to both children and caregivers when they can progress through the same intermediate steps each time. In addition, smaller incremental changes (e.g., being able to tolerate the food on the same plate or touching their skin) can increase children’s sense of mastery and increase caregivers’ ability to feel effectual. The program also is unique in its approach in ensuring families provide modeling for food behaviors to make mealtimes more natural, rather than focused on child compliance or bites swallowed. This feeding program appeared to decrease caregiver-reported feeding stress, as intended. One strength of this feeding program is that it addresses the family system impacted by feeding problems and not just the specific feeding mechanics and behavior of the child. Consistently using an escape extinction model and rewards system or operant conditioning model at each meal with children, as in many other types of feeding interventions, has the potential to be difficult to maintain over time ( ). In our intervention, the goal is focused more on meeting a child where they are, keeping interactions enjoyable and fun, stopping at the food hierarchy level when they have reached the upper limit of tolerance for that meal, and revisiting the food through additional exposures at another time until the child is habituated and even enjoying that level of exposure. The family focuses on positive modeling and increased conversations during mealtimes that are more naturalistic, rather than focus on just the child with feeding problems. This approach has the potential to decrease the extent to which feeding problems impact the family. The results of our analyses suggest that this approach is related to decreases in caregiver stress and the negative impact of feeding problems on the family. It is particularly interesting that caregivers of children with developmental disabilities reported a significant decrease in caregiver strain, a highly desirable outcome given the multiple demands these caregivers are faced with. Conversations can help increase children’s vocabulary, and family mealtimes have also been linked to positive mental health and academic benefits ( ; ; ). By decreasing the need for meals to focus on compliance, families can focus more on these joyful types of conversations and playful interactions that can foster positive child-parent interactions. This study is also unique in reporting results on the use of a group treatment format and use of peer modeling as a component to treatment. Children often learn from each other and it was hypothesized that it could be beneficial for children to see other children also sharing similar struggles with food and to be able to practice the steps to eating together. Group treatment also has the advantage for caregivers. Many caregivers with children with feeding disorders experience stress and social isolation (e.g., ). The group format allows caregivers to share their experiences with other caregivers who understand the level of stress and strain children’s feeding problems can cause. Another strength of this study is its inclusion of children with diverse medical and diagnostic backgrounds. Approximately 45% of the participants have an autism spectrum disorder. Children with autism spectrum disorders can sometimes have difficulties with unstructured periods at school such as lunchtime, and selective eating and feeding problems may exacerbate difficulties at lunchtime. This treatment approach allows these patients the experience of meal periods that include other children. In addition, most children eat some meals with other children in the school setting such that the feeding group could imitate the experience of eating with peers and help with generalizability. Additionally, this study begins to address some of concerns regarding numbers of subjects, use of caregiver questionnaires, description of maladaptive behaviors, and social validation. This study utilizes a multimethod, multireported approach. Both caregiver reports, as well as objective behavioral measurements in sessions, were recorded and compared. Limitations and Future Directions This retrospective research design has limitations. First, this study would have been strengthened by being conducted first as a feasibility study that gathered feasibility measures to be in line with the NIH Stage Model for Behavioral Intervention Development ( https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dbsr/nih-stage-model-behavioral-intervention-development ). There are several aspects that suggest the program would be feasible. The SOS Approach, a component of the Picnic Group, has reported on costs of running the SOS Approach program ( ). The program has offered courses and workshops to providers for decades, which suggests acceptability to providers and the ability to disseminate the intervention. The Get Permission Approach, another component of the Picnic Group, similarly offers workshops and courses to providers, suggesting acceptability and dissemination possibilities ( www.getpermissionapproach.com ) . A retrospective study of 10 participants in a Food Chaining intervention showed efficacy in the community setting ( ). Another intervention component was Satter’s Division of Responsibility and Eating Competence Model, which also trains other professionals and offers continuing education credits, suggesting acceptability and ability to disseminate the intervention ( https://www.ellynsatterinstitute.org/ ). Further, a feasibility study examining an adaptation of Satter’s work showed the adaptation was acceptable and feasible ( ). While this study did not collect feasibility data, it provides significant value. First, one of the main reasons to start with a feasibility study is that some interventions may require too many resources to be implemented in real-world settings ( https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dbsr/nih-stage-model-behavioral-intervention-development ). At our pediatric hospital outpatient setting, groups typically run 3 times a year and this study examines groups over a 10-year period. This history suggests this program can be implemented in a real-world community setting with community-level therapists to work with patients who had a mix of commercial and public insurance, as well as a breadth of diagnoses. This history suggests that adequate resources were available to implement the program, as occupational therapists, speech language pathologists, dietitians, and psychologists were able to implement the program during this period and the program is sustainable. Another reason to initially conduct feasibility studies is that it can be difficult to generalize a treatment from a research study to the community setting, and treatment outcomes may weaken in community setting with community providers ( ). The positive outcomes of this retrospective study in a real community setting with community providers is promising, as one might expect a study conducted under more robust research conditions with a higher level of fidelity may yield stronger outcomes. This current study provides a first step to suggesting this type of group treatment can be implemented and yield positive outcomes when implemented in a community-based setting with community-based providers. This study takes a first step at examining the potential impact of an interdisciplinary group format using systematic desensitization in a playful social setting and a family-centered and classical conditioning approach by increasing pleasurable food experiences to increase food repertoire. Future studies should gather feasibility data. They can compare progress of children in the group setting to children on a waitlist to examine impact of intervention versus natural maturation. Future studies might also compare long-term outcomes between randomized groups where children underwent this current interdisciplinary group with systematic desensitization, and group where children underwent a more operant conditioning and escape extinction model. Several articles have discussed the need for randomized, controlled trials for therapeutic approaches to address pediatric feeding difficulties ( ; ). Future studies could examine long-term follow-up and further analyze cost-effectiveness of this program. Third, this study’s outcome measures were broad, such that it is hypothesized that decreased caregiver stress was related to increased emphasis on positive experiences of food at mealtimes, changes to the conceptualization of the responsibility of caregivers at mealtime, change of their roles from command enforcers, and targeted strategies to address cognitions, emotions, and behaviors of the caregivers. The study also examined children’s tolerance of new foods. However, specific item outcomes were not directly compared. Further studies can examine outcomes such as tube dependency, variety of food repertoire, oral motor skills, as suggested by . In addition, future studies can directly examine factors that potentially mediate or moderate the impact of treatment, such as parenting style, other concurrent interventions, and patient medical status to help elucidate what works for whom the best, and which specific components of the treatment are most robust. Peripartum depression (PPD) is formally defined as an episode of unipolar major depressive disorder (MDD) with onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after childbirth. However, a recent review pointed out several specificities of PPD compared with MDD, such as distinctive risk factors (e.g. ovarian tissue expression, premenstrual syndrome), symptomatology (less sad mood, lower suicidal risk, but predominant anxiety, irritability, obsessive thoughts and guilt about not being a good mother) and wider cross-cultural variety. Furthermore, it showed that PPD can occur up to 1 year postpartum. Therefore, for the purpose of this document, a broad definition of PPD was adopted, including the pregnancy and the postpartum period up to 1 year after childbirth. We use the terms ‘depression during pregnancy’ when we refer to prepartum depression only and ‘postpartum depression’ when referring only to depression after childbirth. PPD global prevalence and its impact The prevalence of PPD varies across countries and regions, and there are several factors that influence its occurrence. According to comprehensive meta-analyses, the overall global prevalence rate of depression during pregnancy is 20% and that of postpartum depression is 17.4%. PPD has many adverse effects, and a systematic review of 122 studies documented the negative impact of PPD on mother, infant and the mother–infant relationship. Maternal depression has, completely justifiably, been called a ‘thief that steals motherhood’. In addition to the consequences of PPD for the mother, the child/children and their family, it is important to note that PPD has significant economic costs to society. In an economic report about the lifetime costs of PPD and anxiety, the estimated total cost is more than £75 000 (about €88 000 in 2024) per woman diagnosed with PPD. Limitations of existing guidelines To prevent PPD and offer timely screening followed by appropriate treatment, it is crucial to have clinical practice guidelines to provide instruction on all these steps, from prevention to screening, and treatment and addressing the different evidence-based options available. A recent systematic review of clinical guidelines relating to PPD, which includes guidelines such as those provided by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), has revealed a significant inconsistency in recommendations. Furthermore, most analysed guidelines demonstrated a high level of bias. Also, information on prevention was scarce. Regarding treatment, most clinical guidelines were focused on pharmacological treatment, less on psychological treatment, and even more rarely on other treatment options, such as non-invasive brain stimulation and alternative and complementary therapies. Also, none of the existing guidelines, including the most recent ones by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, , specifically focus on PPD. Aims Considering that PPD is a highly prevalent mental health disorder in the peripartum period, and given a large amount of new evidence in this field and a lack of consistency in the previous guidelines with a high risk of bias, the aim of this paper was to collect and summarise the current evidence on the effectiveness of the prevention, screening and treatment options for PPD, and offer up-to-date, evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for PPD management. Method The evidence-based guidelines were developed by the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) of Riseup-PPD Cost Action based on the World Health Organization (WHO) manual for developing guidelines for clinical practice. The WHO Handbook is one of the reference manuals for the implementation of a clinical guide. Following the WHO recommendations, this group was multidisciplinary, formed by a group of 14 specialists in the field of peripartum mental health, from different fields of expertise (psychiatry, psychology, pharmacology, obstetrics, ethics, social work, information science), and also including a patient representative association and members from 12 different countries. Literature search Ten patient/population, intervention, comparison and outcomes (PICO) questions were developed (see Supplementary Material 1 ). Six search strategies were developed to address the PICO questions. In the situation where there was an umbrella review available (and with one of the GDG members as an author), the evidence of that review was analysed to develop the recommendations. If this umbrella review was out of date, the GDG conducted an additional search for new systematic reviews. If there was no umbrella review available, a new search was performed. All searches were performed in five databases [CINAHL (Ebsco), the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Medline (Ebsco), PsycInfo (Ebsco) and Web of Science (Clarivate)], from 2010 until 2023, using title/abstract keywords and controlled vocabulary, as appropriate, in English. Search strategies are available in Supplementary Material 1 . Study selection Evidence for inclusion was limited to systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Study selection and data extraction were performed by at least two authors, with conflicts over inclusion adjudicated by a third author. Search strategies and PRISMA diagrams for each question are available in the appendix to the published guidelines. A quality assessment was performed using the AMSTAR 2 tool. The current document summarises the key questions and the recommendations from the ‘Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guidelines for Prevention, Screening and Treatment of Peripartum Depression’. Further background information and the supporting evidence for each recommendation can be found in the full version of the guidelines available from https://www.riseupppd18138.com/clinical-practice-guidelines.html . Prevention of PPD Are interventions effective in preventing PPD among women from the general population, non-depressed, with no known risks or not identified as at risk for developing PPD? The effectiveness of several interventions was examined: psychological and psychosocial interventions, antidepressant medication, dietary supplements and physical activity. Pregnant and postpartum women identified as at risk for developing PPD should receive psychological and psychosocial interventions for the prevention of PPD. Pregnant and postpartum women with no known risks for developing PPD could benefit from receiving psychological and psychosocial interventions for the prevention of PPD. Associated with efficacy studies, cost measures such as maternal/parental outcomes (e.g. morbidity, health-related quality of life, health services use, return to work), infant/child outcomes (e.g. preterm birth, infant mortality, vaccination, neurodevelopmental, socio-emotional and behavioural problems, school performance) and parenting outcomes (e.g. maltreatment of children and intimate partner violence (IPV)) should determine whether such types of interventions are worthwhile to implement ( ). Some recommended types of such preventive interventions for women at risk and women with no known risks include interventions based on cognitive–behavioural therapy (CBT) and interpersonal therapy (IPT), postpartum professional-based home visits, midwifery redesigned postnatal care and postpartum lay-based telephone support. – Pregnant and postpartum women with subclinical PPD symptoms could benefit from psychological and psychosocial interventions for the prevention of PPD. Some recommended types of such interventions include interventions based on CBT and IPT and parent–infant interaction treatment. Concerning pharmacological intervention to prevent PPD, there is one Cochrane review that investigated if antidepressant initiation after delivery could prevent PPD. The review includes two randomised controlled trial (RCT) studies with 73 women. The relative risk for postpartum depression was 0.14 (95% CI: 0.02–1.07, p = 0.058) in the sertraline arm versus placebo, but there was no difference between nortriptyline and the placebo group. Because of low statistical power and scarce evidence, a conclusion on the effectiveness of antidepressants in the prevention of PPD cannot be made. There is no available evidence about the efficacy of antidepressant initiation during pregnancy for prevention of depression during pregnancy. There is limited evidence to recommend that dietary intake influences the risk of PPD. – Pregnant and postpartum women could benefit from physical activity for the prevention of PPD. Some recommended types of physical activity include stretching, Pilates and aerobics. In addition, at least 90 min of physical activity per week are recommended for prevention of PPD. , Screening for PPD When examining the evidence of screening programmes in detecting and/or reducing PPD, eight systematic reviews were included, out of which two were meta-analyses. These systematic reviews had different criteria for inclusion, such as type of studies considered, period of screening (during pregnancy and/or postpartum period), type of setting, delivery agents, provision of dedicated training for the involved professionals and enhanced care combined to screening. The instrument most often used was the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Screening both in mid- to late pregnancy and between 2 and 3 months postpartum was reported. The scales used could be filled out by the participants themselves, or together with a healthcare professional. As no comparison was performed between these alternatives, no clear recommendation on exact timing of screening or exactly which tool to use can be made based on this review. Overall, the evidence suggests a reduction in PPD and improved uptake rates of referral interventions among peripartum women undergoing screening programmes in healthcare settings. The direct evidence showed that screening women for depression during pregnancy and/or in the postnatal period may reduce depressive symptoms and reduce the prevalence of depression at follow-up in a given population, particularly in the presence of additional interventions combined to screening (e.g. treatment protocols, care management, availability of personnel trained on screening and on providing PPD counselling and/or treatment) provided on-site ( ). The indirect evidence showed that screening instruments could identify pregnant and postpartum women who need further evaluation and may need treatment. Patient satisfaction with PPD screening programmes was high in the five studies evaluating this aspect. Two studies , included in the systematic review by Waqas et al evaluated cost-effectiveness and found screening interventions to be cost-effective. PPD screening should only be offered with adequate systems in place to ensure that women with positive screening results are appropriately diagnosed and treated according to evidence-based guidelines, by trained healthcare providers, within a specified time period, or promptly referred to a setting that can provide that level of care. Evidence on cost-effectiveness and acceptability should encourage policymakers and clinicians to address the challenges of introducing universal screening for PPD. These include, at least, ensuring the training of clinicians involved, supporting the collaborative care model between primary care and mental health professionals, the availability of crisis intervention and the provision of appropriate treatment for women with a confirmed diagnosis of PPD. Are screening programmes effective in detecting the presence of risk factors for vulnerability to depression? We specifically examined whether screening programmes were effective in detecting the presence of risk factors for vulnerability to depression. For this question, we identified two systematic reviews: Felice et al focused on four RCTs on pregnant women screened by a psychosocial assessment tool, for example, ALPHA or ANRQ, including known risk factors for PPD. When compared to routine care, psychosocial assessments were found to be sensitive to detect risk factors associated with postpartum depression. Results from three studies reported no statistically significant differences in postpartum depression. One study did not report on depression outcomes. One study found higher referral rates to social services in the intervention group, while another showed higher social support postpartum. The level of evidence varied. In the systematic review on screening for IPV by Feltner et al, five studies focusing on IPV screening among peripartum women showed lower IPV rates postpartum in the screening group. Fewer postpartum depressive symptoms in the intervention group were reported in some studies. It is important to note that evidence based solely on systematic reviews was scarce in this area. Further research to assess efficacy, feasibility, acceptability, preferences and cost-effectiveness of such high-risk assessment programmes is warranted. Treatment of PPD Psychological treatment of PPD Are psychological interventions effective in treating PPD? We identified 15 systematic reviews. – Fourteen were consistent in showing that psychological interventions were effective in treating depressive symptoms during pregnancy and postpartum compared to no treatment ( ). With respect to different psychological approaches, the evidence is strongly related to CBT. The evidence for effectiveness of CBT’s third-wave techniques (behavioural activation, mindfulness-based techniques and acceptance-commitment therapy (ACT)) was weak. Furthermore, the evidence of IPT effectiveness was also weak. In summary, psychological treatments, especially CBT, are effective in treating PPD and should be used. However, a Cochrane review showed superiority of antidepressant medication compared to placebo especially in women with moderate-to-severe depression. Pharmacological treatment of PPD Are pharmacological interventions effective in treating PPD? With regards to the effectiveness of antidepressant medication in PPD, the evidence is limited as double-blinded placebo-controlled randomised drug trials are difficult to conduct in pregnant and breastfeeding women because of ethical considerations. However, a Cochrane review showed superiority of antidepressant medication compared to placebo especially in women with moderate-to-severe depression. There are numerous meta-analysis and systematic reviews investigating the safety of antidepressant medication use in pregnancy with regards to malformation risk and other outcomes in exposed children. The evidence is quite strong that antidepressants in general are not major teratogens. In different drugs, there were hints of a mildly increased malformation risk, but the causality is not clear and rather doubtful. However, there is sufficient evidence that untreated depression can have negative impacts on exposed children; therefore, the risk of not treating depression should always be discussed and weighed against potential effects of the medication. Discontinuation of existing antidepressant treatment is not recommended in women with a history of severe and recurrent disorder because of increased risk of relapse. However, to reduce potential negative effects of the medication, women should be treated with monotherapy and the lowest effective dose, if possible. Regular therapeutic drug measurements (TDMs), that is, measurement of the antidepressant blood concentration at designated time intervals, can be helpful in achieving those goals of optimal dosing, as there is evidence of changes in pharmacokinetics during the three trimesters of pregnancy. As clinicians and affected individuals are often reluctant to increase dosages in pregnancy even if depressive symptoms are not sufficiently controlled, TDM can support informed shared decision-making. However, prospective studies to investigate if TDM in pregnancy leads also to an improvement in clinical outcome are still lacking. As most likely the depression of the mother alone increases the risk for pregnancy and birth complications, affected women should give birth in hospitals with specialised neonatal care units. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has licensed the first specific medication for PPD treatment, the neurosteroid brexanolone. The evidence of two meta-analyses shows that brexanolone is more effective than placebo and more rapidly acting than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in treating PPD. , To date, there is no evidence that specific antidepressants would be more effective in women in pregnancy and/or postpartum. In summary, antidepressant medication should always be prescribed after careful assessment of the individual risk–benefit ratio, including previous history, current severity of symptoms, patients’ preference and availability of alternative treatments ( ). Non-invasive brain stimulation interventions for PPD Four types of non-invasive brain stimulation interventions were considered: repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), specifically transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and bright light therapy (BLT) ( ). Are non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) interventions effective in reducing depressive symptoms during pregnancy and in the postpartum period pre–post treatment or when compared with other intervention or no intervention? Although the evidence for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is promising, the literature shows very low to low evidence of effectiveness both as a stand-alone and coadjuvant treatment with pharmacotherapy in reducing PPD symptoms during pregnancy and postpartum. The low level of evidence is caused by the weak design of the clinical studies and the lack of adequately powered RCTs. – During pregnancy, only half of the studies showed rTMS efficacy as an adjunctive treatment to medication in pre- to post-intervention analysis; response and remission rates ranged between 38.8% and 81.8% and 18.8% and 61.1%, respectively. However, this effect was not significantly different compared to sham control groups. In the postpartum period, rTMS efficacy results are promising. Hence, despite the heterogeneity of treatment protocols, the evidence is of higher quality with optimal information size and large effect sizes (standardised mean difference (SMD) = −1.02 (95% CI [−1.37 to −0.66], I 2 = 83%). Evidence on adverse effects for the foetus during pregnancy show no association with the intervention and, for the women, adverse effects reported were equivalent to those found in the general population. Considering the literature on the safety profile of rTMS in the general population, severe adverse effects are unlikely in the postpartum stage. Acceptability and feasibility data suggest women’s openness to treatment both during pregnancy and postpartum, , , particularly when using shorter protocols such as theta burst stimulation. Although the evidence for rTMS is still scarce for PPD, considering the effectiveness on depressive symptoms in the general population and the safety profile, our recommendations consider that if rTMS is accessible and available, it can be an alternative treatment for pregnant or postpartum women with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, according to their clinical condition, values and preferences. There is some evidence

in the general population, severe adverse effects are unlikely in the postpartum stage. Acceptability and feasibility data suggest women’s openness to treatment both during pregnancy and postpartum, , , particularly when using shorter protocols such as theta burst stimulation. Although the evidence for rTMS is still scarce for PPD, considering the effectiveness on depressive symptoms in the general population and the safety profile, our recommendations consider that if rTMS is accessible and available, it can be an alternative treatment for pregnant or postpartum women with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, according to their clinical condition, values and preferences. There is some evidence showing the benefit of tES as a stand-alone or coadjuvant with psychotherapy in improving depressive symptoms during pregnancy. Within tES, tDCS is the most studied strategy, showing a highly tolerable and safe profile for women and the foetus. Surprisingly, in the postpartum period, there is only one case report available in the literature showing a positive effect of tDCS to improve depressive symptoms. Therefore, despite tDCS’s benign effects in the general population, there is not enough data to make a recommendation on the use of tES postpartum. Because of ethical concerns, the literature on the efficacy of ECT in PPD during pregnancy is of low quality, with no RCTs available, relying only on case series and case studies. , , All articles report patients with severe PPD, presenting life-threatening conditions. Adverse effects on the mother were reported in about 27–52.4% of patients and include vaginal bleeding, uterine contractions, abdominal and pelvic pain, miscarriage, preeclampsia and premature birth and spontaneous abortion when the treatment was delivered during the first trimester. – Caesarean, premature labour and uterine contractions associated with treatment are the most common obstetric complications associated with ECT treatments delivered in later semesters. Moreover, neurocognitive assessment after ECT extracted from one single study suggests that the maximum number of ECT sessions before achieving cognitive decline should be nine. Rates ranging between 27.7% and 57.1% of significant adverse outcomes to the foetus and the child are also reported. These figures warrant strict supervision of ECT during pregnancy, which should be held preferably in a hospital setting by experienced healthcare teams. The literature on using ECT in the postpartum , encompasses case reports and retrospective and observational studies, observing postpartum women in the context of severe psychiatric disorders, unresponsive to other treatments. A percentage of 28% of adverse events was reported and remission rates were between 76.9% and 92%. Therefore, despite the potential for serious adverse effects and complications, particularly during pregnancy and delivery, the benefits of ECT seen in the clinical practice often outweigh these risks in urgent, life-threatening situations where conventional treatments have failed. While the GDG recognises the very low level of evidence, we acknowledge the clinical experience of our experts, strongly recommending ECT where it can be a lifesaving intervention, which is the case with life-threatening, therapy-resistant severe perinatal depression (PPD). Note, however, that ECT treatments, particularly during pregnancy, should be held in hospital settings close to a labour ward, by experienced healthcare teams including an obstetrician, and warranting strict supervision, including cardiotocography monitoring. Finally, the literature on the efficacy of BLT in reducing depressive symptoms in pregnant women , , – reports inconsistent findings and the quality of the evidence is very low given the reduced number of women and the moderate risk of bias of the studies. As for BLT postpartum, only one study is available observing the effect of improving depressive symptoms in postpartum women. Therefore, there is no evidence on the efficacy of BLT that allows us to provide recommendations either during pregnancy or the postpartum period. Complementary and alternative therapies (CATs) for PPD We considered eight types of CATs for PPD: fatty acids, physical exercise, yoga, massage, peer support, acupuncture, Chinese herbs and music therapy ( ). Are CATs effective in reducing depressive symptoms during pregnancy and in the postpartum period pre–post treatment or when compared with other interventions or no intervention? Overall, the quality of the current evidence about the effectiveness of fatty acids in reducing depressive symptoms in pregnant and postpartum women is low to moderate, given its inconsistency and risk of bias. However, the direction of findings suggests their potential effect in mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, when compared to placebo, but not in severe symptoms. Adverse effects associated with fatty acids are likely to be trivial. – Physical exercise for pregnant women with depressive symptoms encompasses low-to-moderate or moderate-to-vigorous dancing, walking, aerobic exercise, stretching and relaxation. Although the available literature on the efficacy of physical exercise on depressive symptoms during pregnancy is of low quality, it shows a beneficial effect. Furthermore, whereas adverse effects of exercise interventions in pregnancy are absent for healthy pregnant women, physical exercise is counter indicated in pregnant women with several health conditions. The American College of

effect in mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, when compared to placebo, but not in severe symptoms. Adverse effects associated with fatty acids are likely to be trivial. – Physical exercise for pregnant women with depressive symptoms encompasses low-to-moderate or moderate-to-vigorous dancing, walking, aerobic exercise, stretching and relaxation. Although the available literature on the efficacy of physical exercise on depressive symptoms during pregnancy is of low quality, it shows a beneficial effect. Furthermore, whereas adverse effects of exercise interventions in pregnancy are absent for healthy pregnant women, physical exercise is counter indicated in pregnant women with several health conditions. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) advises against aerobic exercise for pregnant women with certain conditions, such as hemodynamically significant heart disease, restrictive lung disease, incompetent cervix/cerclage, risk of premature labour in multiple gestations, persistent bleeding in the second or third trimester, placenta praevia, ruptured membranes and pregnancy-induced hypertension. In addition, the ACOG suggests that aerobic exercise may be inappropriate for pregnant women with severe anaemia, unassessed maternal cardiac arrhythmia, chronic bronchitis, extreme obesity, very low body weight (body mass index <12), lack of physical activity, intrauterine growth restriction, uncontrolled hypertension/preeclampsia, orthopaedic limitations, uncontrolled type II diabetes, seizure disorders, thyroid disease and a history of significant cigarette smoking. The ACOG also highlights specific warning signs, such as vaginal bleeding, shortness of breath before exertion, dizziness, headache, chest pain, muscle weakness, calf pain or swelling (which may indicate thrombophlebitis), signs of preterm labour, reduced foetal movement and leakage of amniotic fluid, which should prompt the immediate cessation of exercise. In the postpartum period, physical exercise (group or individual aerobic, walking and pram walking, whole-body stretching sessions; in-person or through e-health systems) seems to be of benefit in reducing depressive symptoms. However, the heterogeneity of exercise interventions described in the literature results in some degree of uncertainty about the parameters for optimal results. Despite the low quality of the evidence, the literature shows that yoga might be beneficial to improve depressive symptoms during pregnancy in physically healthy women , with unlikely associated risks for the foetus/newborn. This recommendation is cautious, as the literature is unclear regarding symptoms’ severity and is based on low-quality evidence. In the postpartum period there is no evidence of the efficacy of yoga to improve depressive symptoms. , , Although the literature is of low quality, massage might be beneficial to improve depressive symptoms during pregnancy when it is applied by partners or therapists. Given there are currently no studies on the effect of massage in the postpartum period, no recommendation is possible. To date, there is only one study observing the effects of peer support in PPD during pregnancy and therefore a recommendation is not possible. Postpartum, interventions are recommended to be provided by health professionals (mediators) or trained peers who have similarities to the pregnant women and have personal experience of previous PPD. No adverse effects are expected, and rates of satisfaction are expected to be high. Interventions can be delivered individually or in a group, or a combination of the two, and those that are technology-based seem to be more consistent. However, while technology increases accessibility it might also increase inequality with those who do not have the resources or the willingness to use digital alternatives. , The available literature on the use of acupuncture for PPD is inconsistent. , Moreover, electro-acupuncture shows transient adverse effects. No recommendation for the use of acupuncture is possible at the current stage. There is no current literature available on the effect of Chinese herbs in reducing depressive symptoms in pregnancy and a recommendation cannot be presented at this stage. In postpartum depression, Shuganjieyu capsules compared to regular antidepressants (e.g. citalopram, paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline) or in combination (e.g. Chai Hu Shu Gan San and fluoxetine) seem to be promising. , – Although no significant adverse effects were reported, the safety of Chinese herbs for the newborn through breastfeeding is unknown. Given the low quality of the included studies, we weakly recommend Chinese herbs in the postpartum period. Moreover, special caution for St. John’s wort should be made as it limits the effectiveness of many prescription medicines and combining it with certain antidepressants can lead to a potentially life-threatening condition. Currently, the effect of music therapy as stand-alone treatment in depressive symptoms in pregnant women is still unknown and a recommendation is not possible. Postpartum, music therapy (e.g. light music, pure music, lullaby) combined with psychological treatment and pharmacotherapy can improve depressive symptoms, insight, pain, sleep, satisfaction and maternal bonding with no adverse side effects expected. Discussion This paper summarises the 44 recommendations from the Riseup-PPD Evidence-based Guidelines for Prevention, Screening, and Treatment of Peripartum Depression, based on an extensive literature review. To our knowledge, these are the first evidence-based guidelines offering recommendations specifically for the management of PPD, representing a substantial

effect of music therapy as stand-alone treatment in depressive symptoms in pregnant women is still unknown and a recommendation is not possible. Postpartum, music therapy (e.g. light music, pure music, lullaby) combined with psychological treatment and pharmacotherapy can improve depressive symptoms, insight, pain, sleep, satisfaction and maternal bonding with no adverse side effects expected. Discussion This paper summarises the 44 recommendations from the Riseup-PPD Evidence-based Guidelines for Prevention, Screening, and Treatment of Peripartum Depression, based on an extensive literature review. To our knowledge, these are the first evidence-based guidelines offering recommendations specifically for the management of PPD, representing a substantial advancement towards improved and high-quality peripartum mental health care. Although previous guidelines have addressed peripartum mental health, , they have not focused specifically on PPD. Furthermore, the majority of previous guidelines exhibited a high level of bias and provided limited information on prevention, and treatment was mostly focused on pharmacological and less on psychological treatments with even fewer references to alternative options, such as non-invasive brain stimulation and complementary therapies. Because PPD is highly prevalent disorder in the peripartum period, and subject to specific prevention, screening and treatment interventions, it is worth addressing this topic in an exclusive way. This is specifically needed given the recent review showing several specificities of PPD compared to MDD, including the symptom presentation, risk factors and other clinical features. This guide provides a clear path for policymakers. Based on the evidence presented in this guide, several policies should be implemented to improve healthcare for peripartum women. To prevent PPD, protocols should be established to discourage the use of antidepressants as a preventive measure and encourage the participation of professionals in psychological and psychosocial interventions. In addition, population screening for PPD should be conducted for all peripartum women. Currently, the available screening tools are easy to administer and do not incur additional costs as they are openly accessible. This facilitates their integration into healthcare systems. It is important to implement screening practices at some point during pregnancy and within the first months postpartum, and have clear care pathways in place in case of positive screening. Consequently, policymakers should recognise the urgent necessity for primary care and maternal health professionals to receive the necessary training and resources to perform screening procedures. Furthermore, it is essential to establish clear and accessible referral pathways among primary care, maternal health and mental health services. High patient acceptability and satisfaction, cost-effectiveness and a reduction of rates of depression should be considered among the pros of universal screening. On the other hand, some increase in visits is needed focusing on the screening and follow-up (which is counter-balanced in studies by visits needed for treatment and general higher pathology among mothers and children after a full depressive episode that is not timely treated), and a possible transient anxiety after a positive screen among those not suffering from depression could be considered among negative side-effects of universal screening. Healthcare professionals, researchers and other stakeholders should bear in mind that different barriers are preventing peripartum women seeking help for PPD, including psychosocial factors, such as stigma or lack of knowledge, structural factors, such as lack of information about services, and instrumental factors, such as financial restraints. , Healthcare systems should be wisely organised to overcome these obstacles. Several suggestions for future studies arose from the conducted reviews. One notable bias observed in the studies was the absence of randomised controlled studies with universal samples. Studies often focus on specific populations, neglecting typical peripartum women. Furthermore, it is important to note the lack of comparative studies, such as those between psychological therapies or between psychological and pharmacological therapies. Research on the mechanisms that explain why preventive interventions or treatments work (response to treatment) remains scarce. In addition, the long-term outcomes of treatments are still unknown, and further studies are needed. We focused exclusively on women in this study, even though there is growing evidence that fathers can also experience PPD. , Unfortunately, it was not possible to include fathers in our recommendations because of the significant lack of research on effective interventions for them, highlighting a crucial area for future studies. Despite these merits, several limitations of this work should be considered. First, the evidence that was collected is limited to systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Although this option allows for the collection of a high degree of evidence, it has the disadvantage of excluding individual papers, namely RCTs, that have not been included yet in a systematic review because of their recency, or for other reasons. For this reason, there may be individual studies that offer relevant information on the efficacy of some interventions that were excluded from our analysis. With updated literature on novel effective approaches in prevention, screening and treatment, the recommendations should be updated, also. Given the rapid increase in new studies,

For this reason, there may be individual studies that offer relevant information on the efficacy of some interventions that were excluded from our analysis. With updated literature on novel effective approaches in prevention, screening and treatment, the recommendations should be updated, also. Given the rapid increase in new studies, we suggest that the Clinical Practice Guidelines should be updated in 5 years. Also, more studies are needed in respect to socioeconomic context, such as the most recent review on the effectiveness of IPT in low- and middle-income countries. Given that most of the original studies come from high-income countries, but that mental health care services differ between high-income and low- to middle-income countries, further efforts need to be undertaken to implement these guidelines in different socioeconomic contexts and healthcare systems. Since women constitute more than 51% of the European population, their health – both physical and mental – should matter to Europe and its key decisionmakers. These guidelines offer 44 recommendations on prevention, screening and treatment of PPD that should direct PPD management based on up-to-date evidence. It is important to make sure these European guidelines will be adopted at a national level to support the lives of the mothers of the 4 million babies being born every year in Europe.
